title: Find your hours: count your week and run a time audit

say: Find your hours: count your week and run a time audit.
This is the video for Module 1, Understanding Your Time.
Every week has exactly 168 hours. That is 7 days of 24 hours. Nobody gets more.
What differs from one woman to another is how much of that time is already spoken for.

panel.heading: Every week has 168 hours
items: Flexible time: the rest, often leaking away
Energy matters as much as hours

say: Fixed time is time you cannot easily move. Sleep, your job or shop hours, the school run, cooking the main meal, worship services you attend every week.

panel.heading: Every week has 168 hours
items: Flexible time: the rest, often leaking away
Energy matters as much as hours

say: Flexible time is everything else. For most women it is larger than it feels, because it leaks away in small pieces of 10 and 20 minutes.

panel.heading: Every week has 168 hours
items: Flexible time: the rest, often leaking away
Energy matters as much as hours

say: And energy matters. An hour at 6 am after good sleep is not the same as an hour at 10 pm. Use your best hours for thinking work.

say: For example, Ngozi runs a small provisions shop in Enugu and has two children. She writes down her fixed hours with a pencil.
Most adults need 7 or more hours of sleep, so 7 hours times 7 nights is 49 hours.

panel.heading: Ngozi counts her fixed hours
items: School run and market: about 9 hours

say: Her shop is open 9 hours a day, 6 days a week. That is 54 hours.

panel.heading: Ngozi counts her fixed hours

say: The school run and market trips take about 1.5 hours a day for 6 days, so 9 hours.

panel.heading: Ngozi counts her fixed hours

say: Cooking, washing up and laundry take about 2.5 hours a day. Over 7 days that is 17.5 hours.

panel.heading: Ngozi counts her fixed hours

say: Church on Sunday and the midweek service come to about 5 hours.

panel.heading: Ngozi counts her fixed hours
items: School run and market: about 9 hours

say: Her fixed time adds up to 134.5 hours. Take that from 168 and she has 33.5 flexible hours. She had believed she had none.

say: Memory is not reliable, so a time audit means writing down what you actually did, as you go, for one week.
Step one. Choose a normal week, not a festive season.

panel.heading: Run a seven-day time audit
items: Choose a normal week, not a festive one
Fill it in every two or three hours
Be honest about what really happened
Label each block with a category letter

say: Step two. Make a log on a notebook page or phone, in 30-minute rows from waking to sleeping.

panel.heading: Run a seven-day time audit
items: Choose a normal week, not a festive one
Fill it in every two or three hours
Be honest about what really happened
Label each block with a category letter

say: Step three. Every two or three hours, stop and fill in what you did in each block.

panel.heading: Run a seven-day time audit
items: Choose a normal week, not a festive one
Fill it in every two or three hours
Be honest about what really happened
Label each block with a category letter

say: Step four. Be honest. Write phone, TikTok, or chatting with neighbour, if that is what happened. Nobody else needs to see it.

panel.heading: Run a seven-day time audit
items: Choose a normal week, not a festive one
Fill it in every two or three hours
Be honest about what really happened
Label each block with a category letter

say: Step five. At the end of each day, mark each block with a letter. W for work, H for home, C for care, T for travel and waiting, P for phone, R for rest, and S for social.
The key rule is to fill it in as you go. Waiting until night means you forget the small leaks.

panel.heading: Run a seven-day time audit
items: Choose a normal week, not a festive one
Fill it in every two or three hours
Be honest about what really happened
Label each block with a category letter
panel.rule: Fill in the log as you go. Do not wait until night.

say: After seven days, count the blocks for each letter and divide by two to get hours. Then compare with your guess.
For example, Halima, a teacher in Kaduna who bakes cakes, guessed about 1 hour a day on her phone.

panel.heading: Halima: her guess and her log
left: About 1 hour a day on the phone

say: Her log showed 46 blocks of phone time. 46 divided by 2 is 23 hours, about 3.3 hours a day. The gap is 16 hours.
She made one change: no social media before her baking orders are done, using an app timer.

panel.heading: Halima: her guess and her log
left: About 1 hour a day on the phone

say: Cutting two or three of the biggest leaks can free several hours a week. The phone is usually first: phone time is often two to three times higher than people guess.

panel.heading: Three big time wasters, three fixes

cards.d: Set app timers, mute busy WhatsApp groups and reply to messages at two or three fixed times.
One fixed place for each item: a hook for keys, a folder for documents and receipts.
Keep a running shopping list on the fridge or phone and go to market once a week.

say: Searching for things is another. Give every item a fixed home, like a hook for keys and a box file for receipts and school papers.

say: Small market trips for one missing item cost a lot of travel time. A weekly list fixes much of this.
For example, Funke in Ibadan did all three and won back roughly 2 hours a day.

say: Sometimes the problem is energy, not time. Tick these each evening for a week.
If you feel exhausted most days even after rest, or low for weeks, see a doctor or health worker. Ongoing tiredness can have medical causes, such as anaemia.

To remember. Count your fixed hours to find your flexible ones. Log your real week. Fix the biggest leaks first. Do thinking work in your best-energy hours. And start small, with two habits and a 15-minute weekly review.

items: 168 hours a week: count fixed hours to find flexible ones

say: Now it is your turn. Count your week, run your seven-day audit, fix three leaks, and keep two habits for two weeks.
The audit is information, not a judgement, so be kind to yourself. Continue with the lessons below.
